summary:
Caquetá is a department of Colombia and stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition with no surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025, and a Colombian court has ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025, and one report counted 13 trans people killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025 alone. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, welcoming the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that rising killings must be addressed urgently.

Targeted killing of trans people also occurs far from conflict zones. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, on 4 April 2025; the assault was filmed and the video went viral the following day, and she died that afternoon. Police questioned local residents, but no one was arrested even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Her mother, Sandra Borja, stated that her daughter was killed for being who she was, and solidarity events were held in several cities.

Inside Caquetá the threat environment is armed-group control. In July 2024 The Guardian documented armed groups running a "social cleansing" campaign: flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, and further waves of flyers were threatened. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men that she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night. A second trans woman reported that a friend of hers had been killed. Tatiana Cespedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice after receiving death threats from armed men. Armed groups also circulated warnings on phones targeting trans women, and trans women in the department reported fleeing it. Discrimination narrows trans women's livelihoods in Caquetá mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and several reported few options beyond sex work.

Lethal violence against trans people is recorded at scale nationally: 41 trans people were killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.
tangentialFactors:
The pattern is not confined to Caquetá. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans", indicating that flyering as a tactic recurs across departments under armed-group presence.

Lethality is not restricted to territories controlled by armed groups. The killing of Sara Millerey in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín, shows that a trans visitor faces documented anti-trans violence in ordinary urban settings outside the conflict-affected departments, and that investigations into such killings may produce no arrests even with a presidential order.

The national counting base differs between sources: the Attorney General's Office counted 35 LGBTI murders in the five months from January 2025, while media tallies counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025, eight trans people killed between February and April 2024, and 41 in 2023. The categories and reporting periods are not identical, so the figures are not directly comparable.
localsOnly:
Residents change the sex marker on their identification by signing a document before a notary, a procedure open since June 2015 without judicial authorisation, bodily inspection or psychiatric assessment; national documents also carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers.

Trans residents of Caquetá face constrained livelihoods, with discrimination limiting work mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and several reported few options beyond sex work. One trans salon owner was forced to relocate twice after death threats from armed men, and a trans woman and local election candidate was driven out of her town, which bears directly on trans participation in local political life.

Residents live under announced "social cleansing" campaigns that name them as military targets in flyers and WhatsApp messages, and forced internal displacement among trans women is reported in the department.

Conflict-era persecution has been addressed through domestic transitional justice: in July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels and recorded gender persecution as a crime against humanity, a channel through which affected residents can seek accountability. Solidarity events were held in several cities after the April 2025 killing in Bello.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources conflict on the cause of Sara Millerey's death: one account records cardiac arrest that afternoon, while another describes her drowning in a creek after the assault. This is unresolved in the inventory and neither version changes the finding that she died from the attack.

No source in this inventory records any Caquetá-specific deviation from Colombia's national legal framework, so formal legal risk for a visitor is assessed on national law; the department-specific findings here concern the threat environment, not statutory divergence. Whether local police in Caquetá respond to threats against trans people, and with what delay or outcome, is not sourced.

How many trans people have been killed or forcibly displaced in Caquetá specifically is not stated in these sources; the counts given are national (41 in 2023, eight between February and April 2024, 13 in the first quarter of 2025). Whether the July 2024 ultimatums and flyer campaigns continued after that reporting is unresolved.

The status and contents of the comprehensive trans law still before the legislature in 2025, and the practical availability of the November 2025 "trans" and "non-binary" document markers at offices in Caquetá, are not sourced here.
